html:
A small church in Rome near the Tiber, on the ground of the Forum Boarium, the old cattle market, where a rock platform under the crypt may be part of the Great Altar of Hercules. In the 6th and 7th centuries this was the city's Greek quarter, home to merchants from the East and officials of the emperors in Constantinople, and later to refugees from war and from iconoclasm. About 550 a welfare hall for handing out food to the poor was built here. Pope Hadrian I rebuilt it as a church about 780, with three apses at the east end in the eastern manner and a small crypt cut into the rock. Its name may come from a monastery of Constantinople whose monks fled to Rome after the siege of 626. The church still serves Melkite Greek Catholics.

Rooms added on its south side were burned in the Norman sack of 1084 under Robert Guiscard. Popes Gelasius II and Callixtus II renewed the church, and Callixtus consecrated it again in 1123. From that work come the seven-storey bell tower, the porch, the marble choir enclosure, the bishop's throne and the inlaid Cosmati floor with a great disc of porphyry; the Gothic canopy over the altar was added in 1294. A Baroque front of 1718 was stripped away in 1894 to 1899 to bring back the 12th-century look. The sacristy keeps a fragment of an Adoration of the Magi mosaic of 706 to 707, brought from Old St Peter's.

In the porch stands the Bocca della Verità, the Mouth of Truth: a large ancient marble face, thought to be a drain cover showing the sea god Oceanus, moved here in the 12th century. Legend says it bites off the hand of anyone who puts a hand in its mouth and lies. A side altar holds a flower-crowned skull said to be that of Saint Valentine.
